IJ
Ivan Joseph The Grass Bank™ Features
November 12, 2026

I met Everton Weekes in Barbados on April 29, 2007. The pleasure was all mine.

I had gone to Barbados along with two of my friends to watch the WC final which took place the day before between Australia and Sri Lanka. The next day Weekes was releasing his book "Mastering the craft" at a prominent department store and having heard about his greatness from my father who had told me that he had scored 5 consecutive centuries in test cricket, I of course had to meet him. I purchased his book and asked him if I could take a picture with him, which he gladly agreed to. We then chatted for a few minutes. He asked me my name and smiled a gentle smile when I introduced myself and then asked him what it took to become a great batsman. I don't fully remember now what he said but nodded respectfully to his answer. He of course signed the book and gave it to me and I took his leave. That was almost 19 years ago but I still remember that brief encounter with true greatness.

How great was he?

He was part of the legendary 3 W's of West Indies cricket - Worrell, Weekes and Walcott - and together they presented a batting line up that very few before or after could match. Weekes averaged almost 59 in his 48 tests, Worrell averaged 49 and Walcott, 57! That tells a story in itself and perhaps in the history of cricket very few threesomes would have such numbers. Weekes in particular has the second highest ever average among West Indian batters, just below George Headley aka black Bradman who however only played in 22 tests. The peerless Garry Sobers averaged 57 and other greats like Viv Richards and Brian Lara also had 50 plus averages but were well below Weekes average.

Five consecutive centuries in Tests:

There are very few records that stand the test of time. Bradman's average, Murali's wickets and this record by Weekes are possibly the only 3 that will. So let's look at how this record came about. It started in the fourth and final Test of the 1948 series against England at Sabina Park, Jamaica when he made 141. Then on the 1948-49 tour of India he hit 128 in the first Test at Delhi; 194 in the second at Bombay; 162 and 101 in the third at Calcutta before he was dubiously run out for 90 in the fourth at Madras. That is a ridiculous run of scores! And to think that but for that run out he could well have scored a sixth consecutive century! As an aside, the great Sunil Gavaskar came close to that scoring 5 centuries in 4 tests but missed out in the Bangalore test in 1978 after having scored two centuries against Pakistan in Lahore (111 and 137) and then a double against West Indies in Bombay (205 and 73) but after the Bangalore failure he scored centuries in both innings against the West Indies in Calcutta (106 and 183 not out). While it can be argued that Sunny did score the same number of centuries in the same number of tests, Weekes didn't miss out on scoring a century in even a single test during his run of 5 centuries in 4 tests which makes his achievement unique.

In his book he talks about his upbringing and how the family did not have much but that never stopped him from pursuing his passion and with much effort and outstanding performances he reached the very pinnacle of batting. He was for some time the very best batter in the whole world! Rarefied air and as a person who had childhood dreams of becoming a batter, meeting him in person and spending a few brief minutes chatting with him was a perfect fanboy moment.

Cricket was in his genes - his son David Murray was West Indies wicket keeper for a while and his grandson Ricky Hoyte played for Barbados in first class cricket.

In 1995, he was knighted joining both Worrell and Walcott who had earlier been bestowed that honor.

Sir Everton Weekes passed away in 2020 at the ripe old age of 95.

He left an indelible mark in the world of cricket. My all too brief encounter with greatness was something that I cherish.

Sources: Barbados Cricket Association
